module_name: Module G — Search, Planning, and Robotics
description: Problem-solving agents, state-space search, uninformed search (BFS, DFS, UCS), informed heuristic search (A*, Greedy Best-First), automated planning, and autonomous robotics.

topics.name: State-Space Search and Problem Formulation
topics.category: Module G — Search, Planning, and Robotics
topics.definition: State-space search is an AI problem-solving methodology that formalizes a goal-directed task as navigating a graph of discrete states using transitions defined by valid actions.
topics.explanation: A search problem is formally defined by five elements: (1) Initial State: the starting state the agent begins in; (2) Actions: set of possible actions available in a given state Actions(s); (3) Transition Model: result(s, a) specifying the outcome of taking action a in state s; (4) Goal Test: determines whether a given state achieves the objective; (5) Path Cost: function c(s, a, s') assigning a numerical cost to each transition. The solution is an action sequence leading from the initial state to a goal state. Search performance is evaluated on: Completeness (is a solution guaranteed?), Optimality (does it find the lowest-cost path?), Time Complexity, and Space Complexity.
topics.example: The 8-Puzzle game: 9 squares with tiles 1 to 8 and one blank space; states are permutations of tiles, actions are sliding adjacent tiles into the blank space, and path cost is 1 per move.
algorithm_steps: Formulate problem: define state space representation, valid actions, goal criteria, and cost metric
Initialize frontier queue with root initial state node
Initialize explored set to record visited states and prevent infinite graph loops
While frontier is not empty: pop node, test against goal criteria, expand successor child nodes
If goal found, reconstruct solution path by tracing parent pointers backwards to root
advantages: Provides a universal mathematical formulation for game playing, route navigation, and puzzle solving
limitations: Combinatorial explosion: state spaces grow exponentially with branching factor b and depth d: O(b^d)
applications: Game engines (Chess, Rubik's cube, Go) and automated circuit board layout
suggested_followups: What are Uninformed vs Informed Search algorithms?
What is Combinatorial Explosion in search?

topics.name: Breadth-First Search (BFS)
topics.category: Module G — Search, Planning, and Robotics
topics.definition: Breadth-First Search is an uninformed graph search algorithm that explores all nodes at the current depth level before moving on to nodes at the next depth level using a First-In-First-Out (FIFO) queue.
topics.explanation: BFS expands the shallowest unexpanded node first. Properties: (1) Completeness: Yes, guaranteed to find a solution if one exists (for finite branching factor b); (2) Optimality: Optimal if and only if all step costs are identical/constant (e.g. 1 per step); (3) Time Complexity: O(b^d), where b is branching factor and d is depth of the shallowest solution; (4) Space Complexity: O(b^d), because all generated nodes at depth d must reside in memory in the frontier queue. The exponential memory requirement is the primary limitation of BFS.
topics.example: Finding the shortest degree of separation between two users on LinkedIn where each connection counts as one uniform hop.
algorithm_steps: Initialize FIFO queue frontier with initial state node
Initialize explored set with initial state
While frontier is not empty:
Dequeue node from front of queue
If node satisfies goal test, return solution path
For each valid action in Actions(node.state):
Generate child state = Result(node.state, action)
If child state is not in explored or frontier, enqueue child
advantages: Guaranteed to find the shallowest goal in terms of number of steps
Complete: will never get trapped in an infinite cycle
limitations: Catastrophic memory consumption: storing b^d nodes exhausts RAM rapidly on deep trees
applications: Shortest path in unweighted graphs and peer-to-peer network discovery
suggested_followups: Why does BFS have high memory consumption?

topics.name: Depth-First Search (DFS)
topics.category: Module G — Search, Planning, and Robotics
topics.definition: Depth-First Search is an uninformed search algorithm that explores as deep as possible along each branch before backtracking, using a Last-In-First-Out (LIFO) stack.
topics.explanation: DFS expands the deepest unexpanded node first. Properties: (1) Completeness: In graph search with cycle detection, Yes (for finite state spaces); in infinite state spaces or tree search without cycle detection, No (can get trapped in infinite depth loops); (2) Optimality: No, may return a deep, suboptimal solution when a shallower goal exists; (3) Time Complexity: O(b^m), where m is the maximum search depth; (4) Space Complexity: O(b*m), requiring only linear memory to store the active path and sibling nodes. Iterative Deepening Search (IDS) combines the linear memory of DFS with the completeness and shallowest optimality of BFS.
topics.example: Solving a maze by following a single path to the very end until hitting a dead end, then backtracking to the last junction.
topics.formula: \text{Space Complexity} = O(b \cdot m) \quad (\text{Linear in max depth } m)
algorithm_steps: Initialize LIFO stack frontier with root node
While frontier is not empty:
Pop node from top of stack
If node satisfies goal test, return solution path
Mark node state as visited
For each valid child state not yet visited, push child node onto stack
advantages: Minimal memory consumption: linear O(b*m) space compared to exponential O(b^d) in BFS
Finds solutions quickly if solutions are dense and located deep in the tree
limitations: Not optimal: can return long, winding, expensive solution paths
Can get stuck in infinite depth branches without strict depth limits or cycle tracking
applications: Topological sorting and strongly connected component detection in compilers
Maze solving and game tree traversal with alpha-beta pruning

topics.name: Uniform-Cost Search (UCS / Dijkstra's Algorithm)
topics.category: Module G — Search, Planning, and Robotics
topics.definition: Uniform-Cost Search is an uninformed search algorithm that expands the node with the lowest cumulative path cost g(n) from the initial state using a priority queue.
topics.explanation: While BFS guarantees the fewest number of steps, it fails to find the lowest-cost path when actions have variable costs (e.g. toll roads, uneven terrain). UCS expands nodes ordered by g(n), the actual cost to reach node n from the start. It is mathematically equivalent to Dijkstra's Algorithm on infinite or dynamically generated search spaces. UCS is Complete and Optimal provided every step cost is strictly positive (cost >= epsilon > 0).
topics.example: Finding the cheapest airline flight route where flights have variable dollar prices: a 3-layover route costing $250 is expanded before a 1-layover route costing $600.
topics.formula: f(n) = g(n), \quad \text{where } g(n) = \sum_{i=1}^k c(s_{i-1}, a_i, s_i)
algorithm_steps: Initialize Priority Queue frontier ordered by cumulative cost g(n) with root node (g=0)
While frontier is not empty:
Pop node with lowest g(n) from priority queue
If node satisfies goal test, return solution path (Goal test applied on POP, not push)
Mark node state as explored
For each successor child of node:
Compute child.g = node.g + cost(node, action, child)
If child not visited or has lower cost than existing entry, insert/update in Priority Queue
advantages: Guaranteed to find the globally optimal lowest-cost path for arbitrary non-negative step costs
limitations: Expands blindly in all cost contours without directional guidance toward the goal (can be slow)
Stores all frontier nodes in memory, leading to high space complexity
applications: Highway map navigation systems when fuel or toll cost is minimized
suggested_followups: Why is the goal test applied on POP rather than push in UCS?

topics.name: Greedy Best-First Search
topics.category: Module G — Search, Planning, and Robotics
topics.definition: Greedy Best-First Search is an informed heuristic search algorithm that expands the node estimated to be closest to the goal according to a heuristic evaluation function h(n).
topics.explanation: Greedy search uses only heuristic knowledge: f(n) = h(n), where h(n) estimates the remaining cost to reach the nearest goal from node n. Common heuristics include Straight-Line Euclidean Distance for route maps and Manhattan Distance for grid navigation. Because it evaluates only forward distance and ignores accumulated past cost g(n), greedy search can be easily fooled into dead ends and produces suboptimal solution paths.
topics.example: Navigating from Arad to Bucharest using straight-line bird-flight distance: it rushes aggressively toward Bucharest, even if local road terrain detours make the actual travel longer.
algorithm_steps: Define heuristic function h(n) estimating remaining distance to goal
Initialize Priority Queue frontier ordered solely by h(n) with start node
Pop node with smallest h(n)
If goal reached, terminate and return path
Expand child nodes, evaluate their h(child), and insert into Priority Queue
advantages: Often finds solutions much faster than uninformed search by aggressively pruning search directions
limitations: Not optimal: frequently returns suboptimal paths because it ignores path cost g(n)
Not complete in tree search: can get trapped in infinite loops on graph obstacles
applications: Rapid non-optimal pathfinding in video game AI where quick response matters more than perfect routes
suggested_followups: Difference between Greedy Best-First Search and A*?

topics.name: A* Search and Heuristics
topics.category: Module G — Search, Planning, and Robotics
topics.definition: A* Search is an informed, best-first graph search algorithm that finds the optimal lowest-cost path by evaluating nodes using f(n) = g(n) + h(n), combining actual past cost g(n) and estimated remaining cost h(n).
topics.explanation: A* balances UCS and Greedy Search: (1) g(n) is the exact cost to reach node n from the start (prevents meandering); (2) h(n) is the heuristic estimate of cost from n to the goal (directs search toward the target). A* is Complete and Optimal under two conditions: (A) Admissibility: h(n) never overestimates the true cost to reach the goal (h(n) <= h*(n)); (B) Consistency (Monotonicity): for every node n and successor n' generated by action a, h(n) <= c(n, a, n') + h(n') (satisfies triangle inequality, guaranteeing no explored node needs reopening in graph search).
topics.example: GPS navigation: A* calculates route by adding actual miles driven so far g(n) to the straight-line distance to destination h(n), finding the guaranteed fastest route while exploring minimum roads.
algorithm_steps: Initialize open set (priority queue) with start node evaluated at f = 0 + h(start)
Initialize closed set (visited nodes)
While open set is not empty:
Pop node with lowest f(n) from open set
If node is goal, reconstruct path using parent pointers and return
Add node to closed set
For each successor child of node:
If child in closed set, continue
Compute tentative_g = node.g + cost(node, child)
If child not in open set or tentative_g < child.g:
Set child.g = tentative_g, child.h = heuristic(child), child.f = child.g + child.h
Set child.parent = node, insert or update child in open set
advantages: Optimally efficient: no other optimal search algorithm expanding the same heuristic explores fewer nodes
Guaranteed optimal and complete with an admissible/consistent heuristic
limitations: Memory-bound: stores all explored nodes in memory (O(b^d)), leading to out-of-memory errors on massive graphs (solved by IDA* or SMA*)
applications: GPS turn-by-turn navigation (Google Maps, Apple Maps)
Video game character pathfinding (Unity, Unreal Engine)
Robotic arm trajectory kinematics and warehouse AGV routing
suggested_followups: Show me the formula for A* search.
What is a Consistent / Monotonic Heuristic?

topics.name: Automated Planning and Decision-Making
topics.category: Module G — Search, Planning, and Robotics
topics.definition: Automated planning is the branch of AI concerned with the realization of action strategies or sequence of actions by an intelligent agent to transition an initial world state into a goal state.
topics.explanation: Classical planning operates in deterministic, fully observable, static environments using languages like STRIPS (Stanford Research Institute Problem Solver) and PDDL (Planning Domain Definition Language). Actions are formalized using Action Schemas with Preconditions (conditions that must hold in current state) and Effects (add and delete lists updating state variables). Advanced paradigms include Partial-Order Planning, Planning Graphs (GraphPlan), and Hierarchical Task Networks (HTN).
topics.example: NASA Mars Rover planning: Given goal 'Collect mineral sample at crater X by 14:00', the planner plans a sequence of actions: [Unstow_Arm, Navigate_Waypoints, Deploy_Drill, Sample_Soil, Store_Container, Retract_Arm].
algorithm_steps: Define planning domain predicates and action schemas (Preconditions, Add-List, Delete-List)
Specify initial state facts and goal conjunction
Generate planning graph or state-space heuristic (e.g. Fast-Forward FF heuristic)
Search forward from initial state (progression) or backward from goal (regression)
Extract validated, executable action plan
advantages: Generates multi-step, causally linked action strategies for complex real-world operations
Discovers long-horizon workflows that satisfy complex physical constraints
limitations: Classical planning assumes deterministic and fully observable worlds; fails under stochastic real-world uncertainty without replanning
applications: Space exploration missions (NASA Deep Space 1, Mars Rovers)
Automated supply chain logistics and manufacturing assembly scheduling
suggested_followups: What is PDDL (Planning Domain Definition Language)?

topics.name: Robotics and Intelligent Physical Agents
topics.category: Module G — Search, Planning, and Robotics
topics.definition: Robotics is the field of engineering and AI focused on designing, constructing, and programming physical machines (robots) capable of perceiving their physical environment, reasoning, and acting autonomously in the real world.
topics.explanation: Robotic architectures integrate: (1) Perception: sensors (LiDAR, ultrasonic, cameras, IMUs) measuring real-world parameters; (2) Localization and Mapping: SLAM (Simultaneous Localization and Mapping) enables a robot to build a map of an unknown environment while keeping track of its location within it; (3) Planning & Control: inverse kinematics (calculating joint angles to reach a coordinate) and motion trajectory planning; (4) Actuation: motors, hydraulics, and end-effectors interacting physically with objects.
topics.example: Autonomous warehouse robots (like Amazon Kiva) navigating crowded distribution floors via SLAM, picking product bins, and delivering them to human packers.
topics.formula: p(x_{1:t}, m \mid z_{1:t}, u_{1:t}) \quad (\text{Probabilistic SLAM posterior over trajectory } x \text{ and map } m)
algorithm_steps: Acquire sensor data (LiDAR point clouds, wheel odometry, camera frames)
Filter sensor noise using Extended Kalman Filters (EKF) or Particle Filters
Update world map and robot pose coordinates (SLAM)
Compute collision-free path toward destination using A* or Rapidly-exploring Random Trees (RRT)
Send low-level PWM torque signals to motor actuators via closed-loop PID controllers
advantages: Performs dangerous, hazardous, or extreme precision work (deep sea mining, radioactive cleanup, surgery)
Dramatically increases industrial manufacturing throughput and reliability
limitations: The 'Reality Gap' (Sim-to-Real): robots trained in computer simulators frequently fail when deployed in physical reality due to friction and sensor noise
High mechanical hardware costs and physical safety liabilities
applications: Industrial robotic arms (welding, painting, electronics packaging)
Autonomous mobile robots (AMRs) in logistics and vacuum cleaning
Surgical robotics (da Vinci surgical system) and agricultural harvesting
suggested_followups: What is SLAM (Simultaneous Localization and Mapping)?
How do PID controllers work in robotics?
